Mount Vesuvius. A sommo-stratovolcano located on the Gulf of Naples in Campania, Italy, Mount Vesuvius is one of the world's most famous and dangerous volcanoes. It is best known for its catastrophic eruption in seventy-nine AD, which buried the prosperous Roman cities of Pompeii, Herculaneum, Oplontis, and Stabiae under thick layers of volcanic ash and pumice. The preservation of Pompeii provided modern scholars with an unprecedented window into daily Roman life and has become a cornerstone of classical history, archaeology, and the science of volcanology. The eruption was documented by Pliny the Younger, who witnessed the event from Misenum and wrote two letters to Tacitus describing the towering pine-tree-shaped ash column, creating the term Plinian eruption. Pliny's uncle, the famous Roman naturalist and admiral Pliny the Elder, died of suffocation at Stabiae while leading a naval rescue mission to save citizens. Vesuvius also served as the hideout for Spartacus and his rebelling gladiators in seventy-three BC, who camped in the volcano's crater before rappelling down using wild vines to defeat a besieging Roman force. Geologically, Vesuvius is classified as a decade volcano, one of sixteen volcanoes selected for intensive monitoring due to their destructive history and proximity to large cities. The volcano is structured as a double volcano, with the active cone of Vesuvius growing inside the collapsed semicircular caldera of the older, extinct Mount Somma. It remains the only active volcano on the European mainland to have erupted in the last hundred years, and its proximity to the densely populated city of Naples makes it a major modern hazard. Vesuvius erupted most recently in 1944 during the Allied occupation of Italy in World War Two, destroying several villages and damaging dozens of B-25 bombers stationed at a nearby airfield. Vesuvius connects to Krakatoa, a peer active stratovolcano famous for its explosive and destructive eruption, to Mount Pelée, a Caribbean volcano whose 1902 eruption mirrored its deadly pyroclastic flows, and to Mount Saint Helens, a Cascade stratovolcano that experienced a modern Plinian eruption in 1980.
